subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has been taking high-dose prednisone for over a year. She develops truncal obesity, moon facies, a dorsocervical fat pad, purple striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, and hyperglycemia. Her morning serum ACTH is suppressed.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected morphologic change in her adrenal glands?

options.text: Bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia
A functional unilateral adrenal adenoma with atrophy of the uninvolved gland
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
Adrenal medullary pheochromocytoma
Bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy

explanation_correct: Exogenous glucocorticoids are the most common cause of Cushing syndrome. The elevated cortisol suppresses pituitary ACTH, and the loss of trophic ACTH stimulation leads to bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy. This is the hallmark of ACTH-independent, exogenous disease and explains why the adrenal glands are small rather than hyperplastic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia results from chronic ACTH stimulation, as in Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH, not from suppressed ACTH due to exogenous steroids.
explanation_incorrect.B: A unilateral adrenal adenoma with contralateral atrophy is an adrenal tumor cause of Cushing syndrome, but this patient has a clear exogenous steroid history and suppressed ACTH.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage causes acute adrenal insufficiency (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) with sepsis, not Cushing syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: A pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor causing episodic hypertension, not cortisol excess with suppressed ACTH.

educationalObjective: Exogenous glucocorticoid therapy suppresses ACTH and causes bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy, the most common form of Cushing syndrome.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 38-year-old woman has progressive cushingoid features including central obesity, facial plethora, striae, and proximal weakness. Laboratory testing shows an elevated serum ACTH and a high cortisol that fails to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected adrenal morphology in this ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome?

options.text: Bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy
Bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia
A unilateral adrenal adenoma with atrophy of the contralateral gland
Adrenal medullary hyperplasia without cortical changes
Normal adrenal glands with isolated pituitary enlargement

explanation_correct: When ACTH is elevated, whether from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or paraneoplastic ACTH secretion, chronic trophic stimulation of the adrenal cortex produces bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. This is the morphologic signature of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome and contrasts with the atrophy seen when ACTH is suppressed.

explanation_incorrect.A: Adrenal atrophy reflects ACTH-independent causes such as exogenous steroids or an adrenal tumor, in which ACTH is suppressed rather than elevated.
explanation_incorrect.C: A unilateral adenoma with contralateral atrophy is a primary adrenal, ACTH-independent cause; it would show low ACTH, not the elevated ACTH in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex, specifically the zona fasciculata, not the medulla; medullary hyperplasia is not the finding.
explanation_incorrect.E: The pituitary may harbor an adenoma in Cushing disease, but the adrenal glands are not normal: chronic ACTH exposure makes them hyperplastic.

educationalObjective: Elevated ACTH from pituitary or ectopic sources causes bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia; suppressed ACTH causes adrenal atrophy.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 41-year-old woman is diagnosed with endogenous Cushing syndrome. Her serum ACTH is elevated, and pituitary MRI reveals a small adenoma. She asks whether this is a common explanation for her condition.
question: Which of the following statements about her underlying disorder is most accurate?

options.text: It is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall, including exogenous cases
It typically causes adrenal atrophy because ACTH is suppressed
It is usually paraneoplastic and associated with small cell lung cancer
It accounts for the majority of endogenous cases of Cushing syndrome
It is ACTH-independent and would be confirmed with adrenal CT

explanation_correct: An ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma is Cushing disease, which is responsible for the majority of endogenous cases of Cushing syndrome. It produces elevated ACTH and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Note the important distinction: exogenous glucocorticoids are the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall, but among endogenous causes Cushing disease predominates.

explanation_incorrect.A: Exogenous glucocorticoids are the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall; Cushing disease is the majority only of endogenous cases.
explanation_incorrect.B: ACTH is elevated rather than suppressed in Cushing disease, so the adrenals become hyperplastic rather than atrophic.
explanation_incorrect.C: Paraneoplastic ACTH from small cell lung cancer or bronchial carcinoids is ectopic ACTH syndrome, a distinct ACTH-dependent cause rather than Cushing disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cushing disease is ACTH-dependent; evaluation is pituitary MRI, while adrenal CT is used for ACTH-independent disease with suppressed ACTH.

educationalObjective: Cushing disease from a pituitary ACTH adenoma is the majority of endogenous Cushing syndrome, whereas exogenous steroids are the most common cause overall.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 47-year-old man has central weight gain, facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, and new hypertension. His physician suspects Cushing syndrome and wants to confirm hypercortisolism before localizing the source.
question: Which of the following testing strategies is most appropriate for initial screening?

options.text: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, and overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression
Serum ACTH measurement followed by adrenal CT
High-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH stimulation testing
Pituitary MRI and a random serum cortisol
Serum aldosterone and plasma renin activity

explanation_correct: Screening for Cushing syndrome relies on demonstrating excess cortisol: increased 24-hour urinary free cortisol, increased late-night salivary cortisol, and failure to suppress cortisol with an overnight low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone test. Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, serum ACTH and imaging are used to localize the source. These tests avoid the unreliability of a single random cortisol.

explanation_incorrect.B: Serum ACTH and adrenal CT are confirmatory and localizing steps performed after screening establishes hypercortisolism, not initial screening tests.
explanation_incorrect.C: High-dose dexamethasone suppression and CRH stimulation distinguish Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH after the diagnosis of hypercortisolism is already made.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pituitary MRI is a localizing study done after biochemical confirmation, and a random serum cortisol is not a reliable screening test.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aldosterone and renin evaluate primary hyperaldosteronism, not Cushing syndrome.

educationalObjective: Screen for Cushing syndrome with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or low-dose dexamethasone suppression.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has classic cushingoid features, and screening studies confirm hypercortisolism. Her serum ACTH is suppressed.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to localize the source of her excess cortisol?

options.text: MRI of the pituitary gland
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
CT of the adrenal glands
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
CRH stimulation test

explanation_correct: A suppressed serum ACTH indicates ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, caused by exogenous glucocorticoids or a primary adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. The next localizing step is adrenal CT to identify an adrenal lesion. In contrast, an elevated ACTH would prompt pituitary MRI or a search for an ectopic ACTH source.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pituitary MRI is indicated for ACTH-dependent Cushing disease with elevated ACTH, not for suppressed ACTH.
explanation_incorrect.B: High-dose dexamethasone suppression testing is used to distinguish Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH in ACTH-dependent cases.
explanation_incorrect.D: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis searches for an ectopic ACTH source such as small cell lung cancer or bronchial carcinoid when ACTH is elevated.
explanation_incorrect.E: CRH stimulation testing is part of the ACTH-dependent evaluation and is not appropriate when ACTH is already suppressed.

educationalObjective: Suppressed ACTH localizes the evaluation to the adrenal glands; adrenal CT is the appropriate next step.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 49-year-old man with confirmed Cushing syndrome has an elevated serum ACTH. High-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress his cortisol, and a CRH stimulation test shows no further rise in ACTH or cortisol, findings consistent with ectopic ACTH secretion.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to identify the source of excess ACTH?

options.text: MRI of the pituitary gland
CT of the adrenal glands
Bilateral adrenalectomy
Repeat the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

explanation_correct: Elevated ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, which is due either to a pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH from tumors such as small cell lung cancer or bronchial carcinoids. Failure of high-dose dexamethasone to suppress cortisol and absent response to CRH point away from a pituitary source, so CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is used to locate an ectopic ACTH-producing tumor.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pituitary MRI would be appropriate if the high-dose dexamethasone test suppressed cortisol and CRH stimulated it, suggesting Cushing disease rather than ectopic ACTH.
explanation_incorrect.B: Adrenal CT evaluates ACTH-independent disease with suppressed ACTH; this patient has elevated ACTH.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilateral adrenalectomy is a definitive treatment in selected refractory cases, not a diagnostic step to localize an ACTH source.
explanation_incorrect.D: Low-dose dexamethasone suppression is a screening test that has already been exceeded; repeating it would not localize the source of ACTH.

educationalObjective: Non-suppressible, CRH-unresponsive elevated ACTH indicates ectopic ACTH secretion, prompting CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
